title: COPD exacerbation (adult)
subject: respiratory
setting: Emergency department, ward, HDU, ICU, outpatient
summary: Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88 to 92%, short-acting bronchodilators, prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days, antibiotics for 5 days only when sputum is purulent or ventilation is needed, and NIV for respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 45 mmHg or more with pH 7.35 or less). Start LABA+LAMA before discharge.

sections.title: Recognise and grade (GOLD 2026, Rome proposal)
items: Acute worsening of dyspnoea, cough and/or sputum over up to 14 days, often with tachypnoea and tachycardia. Exclude mimics: pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, acute heart failure, pneumothorax, arrhythmia or acute coronary syndrome.
Mild: dyspnoea VAS below 5, respiratory rate below 24/min, heart rate below 95/min, resting SpO2 92% or more on usual oxygen (fall of 3% or less), CRP below 10 mg/L.
Moderate: at least 3 of dyspnoea VAS 5 or more, respiratory rate 24/min or more, heart rate 95/min or more, SpO2 below 92% or a fall of more than 3%, CRP 10 mg/L or more.
Severe: moderate features plus hypercapnia and acidosis on blood gas (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg and pH below 7.35).

Admit if there are signs of respiratory failure (rising respiratory rate, accessory muscles, worsening hypoxaemia or hypercapnia, altered mental state), failure of initial treatment, serious comorbidity (heart failure, arrhythmia) or poor home support.

sections.title: Immediate management
items: Controlled oxygen to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92% (24% Venturi at 2 to 4 L/min, 28% Venturi at 4 L/min, or nasal cannula 1 to 2 L/min) pending blood gas (BTS 2017). If PaCO2 is normal and there is no history of hypercapnic failure needing NIV, target 94 to 98%. Recheck gas 30 to 60 minutes after any change.
Salbutamol with or without ipratropium: one nebulised dose every hour for 2 to 3 doses, or pMDI 1 to 2 puffs every hour for 2 to 3 doses, then every 2 to 4 hours by response. Avoid high SABA doses.
In hypercapnic or at-risk patients drive nebulisers with air, not oxygen, and give oxygen separately by nasal cannula.
Prednisolone 40 mg orally once daily for 5 days. Oral is as effective as IV; longer courses increase pneumonia and mortality risk.
Continue the usual long-acting bronchodilators, or start them as soon as possible. Do not use IV theophylline or aminophylline.

sections.title: Investigations (hospital)
items: Arterial blood gas; repeat after oxygen changes and 1 to 2 hours after starting NIV. A venous gas can track pH and PaCO2 trend.
Chest X-ray, ECG, CBC with eosinophil count, CRP, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose.
Sputum culture if purulent sputum in hospital, frequent exacerbations, severe airflow obstruction or mechanical ventilation (Pseudomonas and resistant organisms are more likely).

Look for pulmonary embolism (found in up to 5.9% of hospitalised exacerbations), heart failure (BNP, echocardiography) and myocardial injury when the picture fits. Do not do spirometry during the exacerbation.

sections.title: Antibiotics and adjuncts
items: Give antibiotics if increased sputum purulence plus at least one of increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume or fever; or a previous positive sputum culture; or need for NIV or invasive ventilation. Point-of-care CRP can help withhold antibiotics in mild cases; procalcitonin protocols are not recommended.

Empirical choice by local resistance: amoxicillin-clavulanate, a macrolide or doxycycline. Duration 5 days (5 days or less in outpatients). In India avoid empirical fluoroquinolones where TB has not been excluded (ICMR).
Pseudomonas risk (frequent exacerbations, severe airflow obstruction, recent hospital antibiotics, ventilated): send sputum first and use an anti-pseudomonal agent per the local antibiogram.
VTE prophylaxis with LMWH or unfractionated heparin for inpatients; monitor fluid balance; treat heart failure and arrhythmias.
N-acetylcysteine may help patients who have difficulty clearing secretions. Advise and support smoking cessation during the admission.

sections.title: Ventilatory support and ICU
items: NIV if any of: respiratory acidosis (PaCO2 45 mmHg or 6.0 kPa or more and pH 7.35 or less); severe dyspnoea with respiratory muscle fatigue (accessory muscles, paradoxical abdominal motion, intercostal retraction); persistent hypoxaemia despite oxygen.

High-flow nasal oxygen for hypoxaemic failure, NIV intolerance or contraindication; in hypercapnic failure NIV is preferred over high-flow (ERS), with high-flow as an alternative if NIV is not tolerated.

Intubate for persistent life-threatening hypoxaemia despite HFNT or NIV, NIV or HFNT intolerance, respiratory or cardiac arrest, reduced consciousness or uncontrolled agitation, massive aspiration or persistent vomiting, inability to clear secretions, refractory shock or severe arrhythmia.
ICU for persistent or worsening hypoxaemia or hypercapnia despite ventilatory support, worsening mental state, need for invasive ventilation, or haemodynamic instability.
NIV can be stopped without weaning once the patient tolerates 4 hours of unassisted breathing. Discuss ceilings of care and advance wishes early, but do not deny ICU on prognostic pessimism alone.

sections.title: Discharge and follow-up
items: Start or optimise LABA+LAMA before discharge; add ICS (triple therapy) after a moderate or severe exacerbation if blood eosinophils are 100 cells/microL or more, most strongly if 300 or more or after hospitalisation.
Check inhaler technique and adherence, give an action plan, and refer for pulmonary rehabilitation to start during admission or within 4 weeks of discharge.
Review within 1 month and again at 3 months with spirometry; reassess need for long-term oxygen then rather than at discharge.
Persistent hypercapnia (PaCO2 above 53 mmHg) 2 to 4 weeks after discharge: consider home NIV with oxygen. Consider CT for bronchiectasis or emphysema after recurrent exacerbations.
Update influenza, pneumococcal, RSV and COVID-19 vaccination and address smoking and biomass smoke exposure.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: High-concentration oxygen or oxygen-driven nebulisers in a CO2 retainer causing worsening acidosis.
Missing pulmonary embolism, heart failure or pneumothorax as the cause of 'exacerbation'.
Steroid courses longer than 5 days and antibiotics without purulent sputum or ventilation.
Delaying NIV in acidotic patients, or discharging on SABA alone without long-acting bronchodilators.

drugs.name: Salbutamol
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mg nebulised (air-driven if hypercapnic) or 100 to 200 mcg by pMDI and spacer every hour for 2 to 3 doses, then every 2 to 4 hours
drugs.notes: Avoid high cumulative doses; monitor heart rate and potassium.

drugs.name: Ipratropium bromide
drugs.dose: 0.5 mg nebulised every 4 to 6 hours with salbutamol
drugs.notes: Stop once long-acting antimuscarinic is restarted.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.dose: 40 mg orally once daily for 5 days
drugs.notes: IV hydrocortisone only if oral route not possible.

drugs.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
drugs.dose: 625 mg orally three times daily (or 1.2 g IV every 8 hours) for 5 days
drugs.notes: ICMR adult doses. Reduce dose if eGFR below 30 mL/min.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days

drugs.name: Clarithromycin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally twice daily for 5 days
drugs.notes: Alternative; check QTc and interactions (statins, warfarin).

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.notes: Only with Pseudomonas risk, after sputum culture; adjust to renal function and antibiogram.
